blocks.output:
Loaded player: Alice
Score: 1000
Health: 95.5

blocks.question: Which class is used to write to a file in C++?
blocks.explanation: ofstream (output file stream) is used for writing to files. ifstream is for reading, fstream does both, and iostream is for console I/O.

blocks.question: What flag opens a file in append mode?
blocks.explanation: std::ios::app opens the file in append mode — new data is written at the end without overwriting existing content.

blocks.question: Which function reads an entire line from a file into a string?
blocks.explanation: std::getline(file, string) reads an entire line from the file stream into the string, including spaces, until it encounters a newline.

blocks.value: Handling Errors Gracefully

**Exceptions** provide a structured way to handle errors without cluttering normal code with error checks. When something goes wrong, code **throws** an exception. Calling code can **catch** it and handle the error. If uncaught, the program terminates.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing try block with throw, catch blocks handling different exception types
blocks.caption: try contains risky code; catch handles specific exceptions; throw signals an error

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — A try block (green) containing code that might throw. An arrow labeled 'throw' points to catch blocks (blue) below: catch(int), catch(std::string), catch(...). Show normal flow continuing after catch. Use exception flow visual with color coding.
try, throw, and catch

Wrap risky code in a `try` block. Use `throw` to signal an error. Use `catch` to handle specific exception types. You can have multiple catch blocks for different exception types. A `catch(...)` catches any exception.

blocks.output:
10 / 2 = 5
Error caught: Division by zero!
Program continues normally.

blocks.value: Multiple Catch Blocks

Catch different exception types with separate catch blocks. Order matters — put specific catches before general ones. The standard library provides exception classes like `std::runtime_error`, `std::invalid_argument`, `std::out_of_range`, and `std::exception` (the base class).

blocks.output:
Invalid argument: Invalid parameter
Runtime error: Runtime problem
Caught int: 42

blocks.value: RAII and Exceptions

RAII works beautifully with exceptions. When an exception is thrown, stack-allocated objects are destroyed automatically (stack unwinding), calling their destructors. This means resources are cleaned up even when exceptions occur — no memory leaks.

blocks.output:
Resource acquired
About to throw...
Resource released (destructor)
Caught: Oops!
Resource was safely released!

blocks.question: What happens to stack-allocated objects when an exception is thrown?
options: Their destructors are called during stack unwinding
They are moved to the heap
blocks.correctAnswer: Their destructors are called during stack unwinding
blocks.explanation: When an exception is thrown, C++ unwinds the stack, calling destructors for all stack-allocated objects in scope. This is why RAII works so well with exceptions.

blocks.question: Which catch block catches ANY exception?
blocks.explanation: catch (...) is the catch-all handler that catches any exception type. It should be the last catch block since it matches everything.

blocks.question: Which keyword is used to signal an error in exception handling?
blocks.explanation: The throw keyword raises an exception, transferring control to the nearest matching catch block. throw can be used with any type: objects, primitives, or pointers.

parts.partTitle: Part 30: Capstone Project — Student Management System

blocks.value: Build Your First Real C++ Program

Congratulations — you've learned all the fundamentals! Now let's build a Student Management System that ties together every concept: classes, inheritance, polymorphism, STL containers, file I/O, and exception handling. This project demonstrates how C++ is used in real-world applications.

blocks.alt: Mind map showing all C++ concepts connected to the Student Management System project
blocks.caption: This project ties together every concept you've learned in the course

Each branch has a small icon.
Project Requirements

Your system should:
1. Store students with name, ID, and GPA
2. Support different student types (Undergraduate, Graduate) via inheritance
3. Add, remove, and display students
4. Search students by ID or name
5. Save data to a file and load it back
6. Handle errors with exceptions
7. Use STL containers (vector, map) for data storage
Main Program with Menu
The main program uses a vector of Student pointers for polymorphic storage, a map for fast ID lookups, and file I/O for persistence. Exception handling ensures the program doesn't crash on bad input.

blocks.value: What You Practiced

**Classes & OOP** — Student base class with Undergraduate and Graduate derived classes
**Polymorphism** — displayInfo() and getType() overridden in derived classes
**Inheritance** — Base student data with type-specific extensions
**STL** — vector for storage, map for fast ID lookups, unique_ptr for memory safety
**File I/O** — Save/load student data to persistent storage
**Exception Handling** — Invalid input and file errors caught gracefully
**Headers** — Separated declaration (.h) from implementation (.cpp)
**RAII** — unique_ptr automatically manages student object lifetimes
Challenge: Extend Your System

Try adding these features on your own:
• Load data from file on startup
• Delete students by ID
• Sort students by GPA or name
• Add a Course class with enrollment
• Calculate class average GPA
• Add input validation for GPA range (0.0 to 4.0)
• Implement a search by name (partial match)
• Add a Teacher class with course assignments
Where to Go Next

You've completed the beginner course! Here's your path forward:
• **Smart Pointers** — shared_ptr, weak_ptr for safer memory management
• **Move Semantics** — Rvalue references and perfect forwarding (C++11+)
• **Lambdas** — Anonymous functions for concise code
• **Multi-threading** — std::thread for concurrent programming
• **Networking** — Boost.Asio or raw sockets
• **GUI Development** — Qt, wxWidgets, or ImGui
• **Game Development** — SFML, SDL, or Unreal Engine C++
• **Competitive Programming** — Master algorithms and data structures

blocks.question: Which smart pointer automatically deletes the object when it goes out of scope?
blocks.explanation: std::unique_ptr is a smart pointer that owns and manages an object, automatically deleting it when the unique_ptr goes out of scope. It implements RAII for single ownership.

blocks.question: Which STL container provides O(log n) lookup by key?
blocks.explanation: std::map uses a balanced binary search tree (typically Red-Black tree) to provide O(log n) insertion, deletion, and lookup by key.

blocks.question: Which C++ feature ensures resources are cleaned up even when exceptions occur?
blocks.explanation: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) ties resource management to object lifetime. Destructors automatically clean up resources during stack unwinding when exceptions occur.
